articles.title: Notes from the
articles.intro: Short, practical guides for building a steady legal-study routine. These editorial examples are not legal advice.

items.title: Read a case with a question in mind
items.excerpt: Start with the issue you are trying to understand, then track how the court moves from facts to principle.
items.body: A useful first pass through a case is purposeful: identify the issue, the rule the court applies, and the reasoning that connects the two. Then write a short note in your own words and check it against the approved report or course material. This is a study method, not legal advice.

items.title: Turn revision into a repeatable routine
items.excerpt: Small sessions, active recall and a clear review plan can make revision easier to return to.
items.body: Choose one topic, set a short timer, close your notes and recall the main points. Afterwards, reopen the material and correct gaps. Save the next action for your next session. FIRE COUNSEL stores the personal study tools in your browser in this preview.

items.title: Make your answer easier to follow
items.excerpt: Use a clear issue, rule, application and conclusion structure, then check each step against the course rubric.
items.body: A clear answer makes its reasoning visible. State the issue, identify the relevant rule from approved course material, apply the rule to the facts, and give a concise conclusion. Use the marking rubric when one is available; do not invent authority or citations.
